enonce_intro_markdown:
The table below shows the demand and supply schedules for maize in a local market:

| Price in FCFA | Demand in Buckets | Supply in Buckets |
|---|---|---|
| 2,000 | 10 | 4 |
| 3,000 | 8 | 5 |
| 4,000 | 6 | 6 |
| 5,000 | 4 | 8 |
| 6,000 | 2 | 10 |

figures.legende: Maize market drawn from the printed schedule: equilibrium at 4,000 FCFA and 6 buckets, and the shortage of 3 buckets created by a maximum price of 3,000 FCFA (model answer to Q5(b)).

Sketches for the three laws of demand and supply: rise in demand (first law), rise in supply (second law), equal rise in demand and supply (third law). Illustrative curves, not data (model answer to Q5(c)).

questions.enonce_markdown:
From the table above, what is the equilibrium price and why?

(2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Equilibrium price = 4,000 FCFA per bucket (1 mark).**

**Why (1 mark):** at 4,000 FCFA the **quantity demanded (6 buckets) is equal to the quantity supplied (6 buckets)**. There is **neither a surplus nor a shortage**, so buyers and sellers have no reason to change the price. At any other price in the table the two quantities are different: at 3,000 FCFA demand (8) exceeds supply (5), and at 5,000 FCFA supply (8) exceeds demand (4).

The equilibrium quantity is 6 buckets.

questions.enonce_markdown:
If the government fixed a price at 3,000 FCFA per bucket;

(i) What name is given to such a price? (2 marks)

(ii) State Four (04) consequences of such a price in (i) above. (4 marks)

(6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Name of the price (2 marks)**

A price fixed by the government **below the equilibrium price** (3,000 FCFA < 4,000 FCFA) is called a **maximum price**, also known as a **price ceiling**. It is meant to protect consumers by making the good cheaper, and sellers may not legally charge more than this price.

**(ii) Four consequences (4 marks, 1 mark each)**

At 3,000 FCFA the quantity demanded is **8 buckets** but the quantity supplied is only **5 buckets**.

1. **Shortage (excess demand).** The shortage is $8 - 5 = 3$ buckets: more people want to buy than there is maize available.
2. **Queues and rationing.** Buyers queue and the government or the sellers must **ration** the maize (for example one bucket per buyer), or sell on a "first come, first served" basis.
3. **Black market (illegal trading).** Some people sell secretly at a price **above 3,000 FCFA** (towards the 4,000 FCFA equilibrium or higher), because buyers are willing to pay more.
4. **Reduced supply and loss of incentive to producers.** At the lower price farmers earn less, produce less maize, or may hold it back or sell it elsewhere, so the shortage may last or get worse.

*Other consequences:* favouritism and corruption in the sharing of the scarce maize, and a fall in the quality of the product. Consumers who succeed in buying benefit from the lower price.

questions.enonce_markdown:
State and sketch on separate diagrams the following:

(i) The first law of demand and supply

(ii) The second law of demand and supply

(iii) The third law of demand and supply

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The three laws describe how the **equilibrium price and quantity** change when demand or supply shifts. In each diagram D0 and S0 are the original curves, E0 is the original equilibrium (price P0, quantity Q0), and the dashed curves are the new curves, giving the new equilibrium E1 (price P1, quantity Q1). The sketches below show all three. (4 marks for each law: 2 for the statement and 2 for the diagram.)

![fig-2](gce-ol-economics-2022-p2-officiel-cameroun_exercice_5_fig_2.png)

**(i) First law of demand and supply**

*Statement:* **When demand increases while supply remains constant, both the equilibrium price and the quantity bought and sold rise.** (When demand falls with supply constant, both fall.)

*Diagram:* draw a downward-sloping D0 and an upward-sloping S0 crossing at E0 (P0, Q0). Move the demand curve **to the right** to D1, with S0 unchanged. D1 cuts S0 at E1 higher up: **P1 > P0** and **Q1 > Q0**. (Example: a rise in people's incomes raises the demand for maize and its price.)

**(ii) Second law of demand and supply**

*Statement:* **When supply increases while demand remains constant, the equilibrium price falls and the quantity bought and sold rises.** (When supply falls with demand constant, the price rises and the quantity falls.)

*Diagram:* draw D0 and S0 crossing at E0. Move the supply curve **to the right** to S1, with D0 unchanged. S1 cuts D0 at E1 lower down: **P1 < P0** and **Q1 > Q0**. (Example: a very good harvest increases the supply of maize and lowers its price.)

**(iii) Third law of demand and supply**

*Statement:* **When demand and supply change at the same time, the effect on price depends on the size of the changes. If demand and supply increase by the same amount, the equilibrium price remains the same (unchanged) and the quantity bought and sold increases.** (If demand increases more than supply the price rises; if supply increases more than demand the price falls.)

*Diagram:* draw D0 and S0 crossing at E0. Move **both** curves to the right by the same distance, to D1 and S1. They cross at E1, which is at the **same height** as E0: **P1 = P0**, while **Q1 > Q0**.

**Note.** These laws build on the basic law of demand (when the price rises, the quantity demanded falls) and the basic law of supply (when the price rises, the quantity supplied rises). Label the axes: price on the vertical axis, quantity on the horizontal axis.
